rows.title: Community Relations
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Critically analyze community-based problems and develop evidence-informed strategies for social change.
Examine the evolution of multiculturalism in the United States and assess its effects on community-police relations.
Analyze historical and contemporary patterns of interaction between communities and the criminal justice system using social and behavioral science frameworks.
Evaluate the challenges, complexities, and inequities that emerge when justice is administered in diverse communities.
objectives: SLO 4: Propose at least one realistic strategy for improving the issue based on research, class discussions, or community examples.
SLO 4: Evaluate existing community responses or programs and explain their strengths and limitations.
SLO 4: Describe possible root causes of the problem in clear, understandable terms.
SLO 4: Identify a real or hypothetical community problem using basic research methods (e.g., observations, news sources, public data).
SLO 3: Discuss examples of how multiculturalism has shaped modern approaches to policing and community outreach.
SLO 3: Explain how cultural values, communication styles, and community traditions influence interactions with public safety agencies.
SLO 3: Interpret simple demographic data to explain changes in community diversity.
SLO 3: Describe key historical moments that contributed to the growth of multiculturalism in the U.S.
SLO 2: Discuss how unequal treatment or inconsistent practices can affect community perceptions of fairness.
SLO 2: Use real or hypothetical case studies to describe why communities may have different levels of trust in the justice system.
SLO : Explain how factors such as race, culture, language, and socioeconomic status influence justice outcomes.
SLO 1: Identify major events and policies that have shaped community and criminal justice system relationships.
SLO 1: Describe basic social-science concepts (e.g., social control, institutional trust, community norms) that help explain community-police interactions.
SLO 1: Summarize similarities and differences between past and present examples of community-justice system relations.
SLO 1: Explain how social, political, or economic changes affect how communities view and interact with the justice system.
SLO 2: Identify common challenges faced by diverse communities when interacting with the justice system.

rows.title: Introduction to Corrections
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Examine the history of punishment and corrections in America and the influence of religion on its formation.
Examine and analyze alternatives to punishment and asses their impact on the criminal justice system and society.
Compare and contrast subgroups and special population clients in correctional facilities and how the challenges each client brings impacts correctional institutions.
Compare and Contrast sentencing practices and the judicial processes for juveniles and adults.
objectives: Analyze the history and theory of corrections, and the development of corrections in the United States.
Identify and describe different types of correctional facilities for adults and juveniles at the local, state, and federal levels.

Evaluate the impact of various crimes on not only the victim and his/her family, but on the offender and his/her family, as well as on the collateral agencies that interact with both during this period.
Examine new and innovative programs being used at correctional institutions and the impact of these programs on clients.
Distinguish between the different clientle housed in correctional settings and the challenges each client brings to correctional institutions.
Critically analyze alternatives to punishment and their impact on the criminal justice system and society.

Identify and analyze the various subgroups and special population clients in correctional facilities and the potential challenges that may arise when managing these groups at a local, state, or federal facility.

rows.title: Security Guard
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Explain the California State policies for Powers to Arrest
Determine proper methods and techniques to protect, resolve conflicts, and overcome resistance.
Accurately observe and report incidents in oral and written forms
objectives: Summarize and give an overview of specific crimes.
Explain in detail the proper techniques or methods used to protect property including search techniques.
Describe and demonstrate proper arrest techniques warranted by the actions of a potential suspect(s).
Assess and explain the steps necessary to resolve conflicts, including the use of force and its application in resolving conflicts.
Explain in detail the techniques used to overcome resistance.
Demonstrate the proper use of forms of restraint such as control holds, handcuffing, and the police baton as well as describe the hazards associated with the improper use of such forms of restraint.
Given case studies and scenarios, evaluate situations to determine if an arrest is appropriate per the California Penal Code.

rows.title: Black Economics
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Evaluate the role of race in the historical economic development of the U.S.
Compare and contrast economic theories and systems from an African centered perspective
Examine the impact of race, class and gender upon African American social and economic life
Evaluate the economic aspects of various theories and social movements for racial equality in America
objectives: Compare and contrast different economic theories and their relation to African-Americans, specifically their social poltical experience in the United States.
Evaluate the status of African-Americans within the economic system, considering the realities and impact of chattel slavery, reconstruction, the great migration and urabanization.
Appraise the various approaches to economic advancement by African-Americans.
Examine the impact of economics on housing, healthcare and education for African-Americans.
Examine and evaluate modern economic trends and policies and the impact on the Black community.

Critically examine and articulate concepts such as race and racism, racialization, ethnicity, equity, ethnocentrism, eurocentrism, white supremacy, anti-blackness, self- determination, liberation, decolonization, sovereignty, imperialism, settler colonialism, exploitation colonialism, xenophobia, intersectionality, and anti-racism as studied in African American studies.

Critically examine, in historical and intersectional context, how struggle, resistance, racial and the quest for justice, solidarity, and liberation, as experienced and, enacted by African American Studies as people of color in the United States are relevant to current and structural issues.

Describe and actively engage with anti-racist, abolitionist, anti-colonial, and anti-imperial thought, issues, practices, and movements in African American Studies as people of color in the United States seeking to build a just and equitable society.

rows.title: The African American Family in the United States
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Explain the role of extended kinship and West African heritage on development of the Black family
Compare and contrast the psycho-sociological theories related to parenting, communication styles, and gender roles of the Black family
Investigate the sociological impact of addiction, domestic violence and employment on the Black family unit
Critique how historical discrimination from slavery, Jim Crow era and 20th centuries movements have influenced the structure of the Black family
objectives: Understand and explain the dynamics between African American men and African American women.
Identify social and psychological propositions about the Black family.
Evaluate the evidence presented in support of propositions or conclusions concerning ethnic stereotypes on role expectations and the impact of wounded self-esteem on the Black family.
Summarize the conditions that lead to the rift between African American men and African American women.
Examine class and the socio-economic impact on the African American family.
Demonstrate the ability to write essays.
Develop a position on an issue including evidence from written source observations using research.
Work in groups as part of a team in gathering resources for presentation.

rows.title: Sociology of African-Americans
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Appraise the class, race, and gender matrix as a sociological tool of analysis.

Examine African American social conditions through a sociological lens by evaluating the political, economic, and social structures and institutions that have and continue to impact Black life. A special emphasis will be placed on issues and topics realating to white supremacy, intersectionality,colonialism and hegemony.
Examine the history of sociology as a discipline with a focus on DuBois and the first urban sociologist who challenged the notioms of racialized segrigation and ethnocentrism.
objectives: Describe how the African-centered approach can be applied to all aspects of life.
Analyze the validity of introductory sociological methods of study.
Examine the major institutions in society and the Black experience within those institutions.
Examine social movements as traditional and historic forms of resilience.
Interpret the impact of Eurocentric hegemony upon Afrocentric sociological thought.
Examine historical and current political, cultural and social conditions of Africans in America using African-Centered sociological theory.
Compare and contrast the varying experiences of being African-American according to gender and class.

rows.title: Psychology of African Americans
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Evaluate African-centered psychological theories as it relates to African Americans and the field of African American studies
Examine African-centered psychological theories and historical efforts of resistance and anti-racist practice for African Americans for healing and liberation.

Critically analyze the intersection of race, racism, and white supremacy as they relate to class, gender, sexuality, sexual orientation, social status, religion, spirituality, national origin, immigration status, ability, tribal citizenship, sovereignty, language, and/or age, in African American communities in the United States.
objectives: DISCUSS THE HISTORICAL FOUNDATIONS ON WHICH AFRICAN AMERICAN PSYCHOLOGY IS BASED.
DESCRIBE AND ASSESS THE ROLES THAT AFRICAN PHILOSOPHY, THE WORLDVIEWS PARADIGM, FAMILY MODELS, AND SPIRITUALITY AND RELIGION HAVE PLAYED IN PROVIDING THE FOUNDATION FOR AFRICAN AMERICAN PSYCHOLOGY.
EXAMINE AND ASSESS THE PSYCHOLOGICAL, CULTURAL AND RACIAL HARM AND/OR IMPACT OF WHITE SUPREMACY, RACISM AND ANTI-BLACKNESS.
EXAMINE AND ASSESS THE PSYCHOLOGICAL RESEARCH ON THE COGNITIVE ATTRIBUTES OF AFRICAN AMERICANS, INCLUDING RESEARCH ON INTELLIGENCE AND BLACK ENGLISH.
EXAMINE AND ASSESS THE PSYCHOLOGICAL RESEARCH ON THE NONCOGNITIVE ATTRIBUTES AND BEHAVIORS OF AFRICAN AMERICANS, INCLUDING RESEARCH ON NONVERBAL BEHAVIOR, RACIAL SOCIALIZATION, AND RACIAL IDENTITY.

DISCUSS POSITIVE PSYCHOLOGICAL RESEARCH ON AFRICAN AMERICANS, INCLUDING RESEARCH ON THE COGNITIVE AND NONCOGNITIVE STRENGTHS OF AFRICAN AMERICANS AND ON FACTORS THAT PROMOTE PSYCHOLOGICAL HEALTH AMONG AFRICAN AMERICANS.
APPLY AFRICAN AMERICAN PERSPECTIVES TO UNDERSTAND AFROCENTRIC ORGANIZATIONAL STRUCTURES, THE ISSUES OF EDUCATIONAL TESTING AND COGNITIVE PERFORMANCE OF AFRICAN AMERICANS, AND THE PROBLEM OF RACISM.
EXAMINE AND ILLUSTRATE HOW AFRICAN AMERICAN PERSPECTIVES CAN BE USED TO ENHANCE THE UNDERSTANDING AND TREATMENT OF MENTAL HEALTH PROBLEMS IN THE AFRICAN AMERICAN COMMUNITY.
Examine the psychological impact of African American psychology as a strategy for anti-racism, resistance and abolition.

rows.title: The Prison Industrial Complex: African American Incarceration
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Evaluate the role of race, gender, age and economic status on the criminal justice system and prison industrial complex.
Examine the role of privatization and private industry profit to increasing incarceration rates.
Analyze the historical and current ideologies, tactics, and resistance movements to racism in the criminal justice system.

Analyze the role of race, gender and socio-economic status in the growth of the criminal justice system.

Analyze contemporary issues, research and policy as it relates to African Americans and the criminal justice system.
Appraise the impact of incarceration upon the African American family and community.
Examine the intersection of education, employment, illegal drugs, police corruption and incarceration rates.
Compare and contrast the effects of the offender’s race and the reaction of the criminal justice system.
Examine the history and current status of race, law and crime and the impact on African Americans.
Examine resistance movements and community organizing efforts on police brutality, political prisoners and increasing incarceration rates.
Analyze the growth and impact of the criminalization of African American youth.

rows.title: Racism in the United States
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Be able to discuss racism using key terms and concepts.
Identify the societal structures in which racism is perpetuated.
Analyze the ways in which racism affects one’s own life.

Examine white supremacy, and structural racism; evaluate the importance of resistance, solidarity and social justice.
Be able to analyze the racial significance and structure of new information and ideas acquired in the future.

Describe and actively engage with African American art as an anti-colonial, anti-racist practice as forms of resistance in the struggle for African American liberation and decolonization against White supremacy, antiblackness, racism, settler colonialism.

Critically analyze how African American culture, music, art, and literature within African American communities reflect struggles for resistance, liberation, and social justice and relate to contemporary structural issues at local, national, and global levels.

Washington and W.E.B. DuBois, Blacks in the military, the developments among black in business, and the cultural developments including music and sports.

Identify the causes and major events of WWII, describe the role and treatment of Blacks during the war, and explain how the war transformed the nature of Black struggles for equality.

Critically examine, in historical and intersectional context, how struggle, resistance, racial and the quest for justice, solidarity, and liberation, as experienced and, enacted by African American Studies as people of color in the United States are relevant to current and structural issues.

rows.title: Environmental Racism and Justice

Develop a basic building project utilizing Revit.

rows.title: Introduction to Art History
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Evaluate creation of art in an historical context with an emphasis on modern life.
Identify broad themes of art located in the context of history and contemporary society.
Analyze properties of art creation in a variety of cultures and periods.
objectives: Apply reasoning skills to successfully recognize and formulate concepts central to the understanding of art. To apply these skills in reading, writing and exploring art texts.
Participate in class discussions critically evaluating viewpoints regarding the study of art.
Compose essays using critical thinking skills, the language of art history, and analysis of artistic form.
Assess and evaluate periods and styles of art coupled with historical analysis, cultural awareness, individual approaches, and cultural ideals.
Examine works of art comparatively to recognize thematic connections, new developments and contrasting methods.
Define stylistic forms of art of a wide range of cultures, artists and periods.

rows.title: History of Modern Art (1800 to Present)
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Employ the vocabulary and concepts of formal analysis specific to the visual arts and art history.
Identify and contextualize artworks according to their formal, iconographic, and social functions.
Analyze, discuss, and distinguish the roles of art, architecture, and the artist from the art historical periods covered in this course
objectives: Delineate the major historical, cultural, and artistic influences upon each of the art periods or styles being presented.
Analyze the contributions of major artists of these periods to the art of their own time and to art of the present.
Develop increasing visual sensitivity and appreciation of works of art from different time periods and styles.
Describe the contributions of women artists and artists of color to modern art and understand their historical status.
Recognize the major museums or galleries in the immediate area and the basis of their collections and special exhibitions.
Demonstrate writing skills in describing the art they are viewing field trip visits as well as those they are studying in class.
Identify, examine, and assess representative works of art and architecture from the art historical periods covered in this course employing appropriate art historical terminology
Analyze, discuss, and differentiate works of art and architecture in terms of historical context and cultural values
Analyze, discuss, and distinguish the roles of art, architecture, and the artist from the art historical periods covered in this course

rows.title: Introduction to Islamic Art
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Employ the vocabulary and terminology specific to the visual material of Islamic art and art history.
Assess the value or relevance of works of art or artists based on a broad view of Islamic culture and art history.
Integrate contributions of Islamic artists; Islamic culture(s), including gender relations; and European and American opinions of Islamic art and culture with shared personal investigations.
objectives: describe the role of material culture in the history of Islamic civilizations
explain tenets of Islamic faith as evident in the art and architecture
identify and discuss problems associated with ethnocentric analysis of art
apply art history terminology relevant to the Islamic world
critically evaluate art and art historical narratives

rows.title: Beginning Drawing and Composition
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Demonstration of basic processes of drawing.
Analysis of issues and aesthetics of composition.
Develop an appreciation for artistic observation and seeing.
objectives: Translate a 3 dimensional object into a 2 dimensional drawing.
Create drawings that demonstrate the basic principles of spatial illusion through the application of linear, atmospheric, and other perspective systems.
Apply a variety of lines and mark making in drawing.
Organize spaces and objects within a drawing according to basic principles of design and composition.
Accurately describe forms and space through gradations of value.
Develop expressive content through manipulation of line, form, value, and composition.
Evaluate and critique class projects using terminology appropriate for the visual arts in oral or written formats.
Examine and describe historical and contemporary developments, trends, materials, and approaches in drawing.
Demonstrate ability with various drawing media and techniques.

rows.title: Special Projects: Drawing
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Develop criteria for critiques and evaluate and analyze artwork; their own, that of fellow students, and that of notable artists
Demonstrate self-directed creative inquiry both thematically and stylistically, in at least three drawings.
objectives: Create and sustain a personal style that is executed with a fully unified and realized composition.
Complete a series of drawings for exhibition or portfolio presentation.
Analyze and critique own and others' work.

rows.title: Beginning Figure Drawing: Anatomy
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Produce drawings in various media reflecting an understanding of basic anatomical function, skeletal and muscular attachment and articulation, surface depiction and proportion.
Complete a drawing of a figure in a particular context, employing gesture, line, value, perspective and the use of various materials to create a dynamic representation of the human form.
objectives: : Create a minimum of 10 drawings demonstrating knowledge of
Perspective
Interpretation of gesture
Beginning Anatomy
: Use a variety of medium and techniques to achieve drawings.
Contour, cross contour
Volume by Shading, crosshatching, etc.
Photorealistic rendering
Basic Pencil techniques
Basic Charcoal techniques
: Identify the parts of the human structure using basic anatomical vocabulary

rows.title: 2-D Visual Design
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Use basic design terminology.
Design and execute compositions, using basic design principles and elements.
Evaluate and compare views and ideas about design outcomes.
objectives: Demonstrate a working knowledge of principles of two-dimensional art, including balance, proportion, repetition, contrast, harmony, unity, point of emphasis, and visual movement.
Identify and apply the fundamental elements of composition, including line, shape, color, texture, value, space, and scale.
Create visual compositions and problem-solving projects that successfully incorporate the basic elements and organizing principles of two-dimensional art.
Make individual aesthetic decisions and judgments related to their own artwork.
Use skillfully a variety of artistic materials, techniques and tools.
Translate ideas and visual experience into images using both formal and conceptual approaches.
Discuss, critique and evaluate their own two-dimensional compositions, as well as those of their classmates.
Discuss and write a critical evaluation of two-dimensional art using the appropriate vocabulary and terminology pertaining to the basic elements and organizing principles of two-dimensional art.
Examine, compare and analyze historical and contemporary examples of two-dimensional art, within a global context.

rows.title: 3-D Visual Design
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Apply basic elements of three-dimensional design including: form, space, line, texture, light, color, time and movement to a variety of projects using paper, wire, found objects, malleable materials, mixed media and time-based art.
Create an artwork that demonstrates ability to translate two-dimensional media into three-dimensional form.
Discuss, describe, analyze and critique three-dimensional works of art through references to the formal elements and principles of design;
objectives: Identify and understand the formal elements and organizing principles of three-dimensional design.

Demonstrate a working knowledge of the fundamentals of 3D design by producing objects, forms, and problem-solving projects that successfully incorporate the basic elements and organizing principles of three-dimensional art.
Use elements of 3D design to create emphasis, rhythm, mood, balance, center of interest.

Critique own work and the work of others through verbal communication in group settings and individually in a written essay, applying appropriate terminology to the visual arts and three-dimensional design.
Analyze how visual elements in their artwork as well as in the work of their peers communicate and contribute to the overall mood and message of the work.
Recognize the presence of specific design elements and principles in works of art as well as in the everyday physical world around them, throughout history and across cultures.
Examine their own artwork by tracing its forms and ideas to art history and contemporary practice.
Compose and problem-solve using a wide range of media which may include wood, plaster, wire, fiber, found materials, paper, and mixed media in an appropriate and safe manner.
Translate ideas and visual experience into tactile forms objects using both formal and conceptual approaches.
Monitor their own creative process, and describe the relationship between visual forms, perception, and meaning.

rows.title: Intermediate Painting
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Create paintings that demonstrate a consistency in mark making.
Identify and discuss cultural and historical painting styles in specific examples.
Identify and discuss compositional techniques in specific examples
objectives: Present finished projects and exercises that demonstrate effective and safe use of their selected choices of materials and techniques.
Present finished artwork that demonstrates a consistency in mark making.
Identify and discuss cultural and historical painting techniques and styles in specific examples.
Identify and discuss compositional elements and relationships in specific examples.
Use appropriate vocabulary to discuss elements and compositional relationships in their own work and to explain and justify their painting solutions.
Discuss and evaluate the painting solutions of others in a constructive manner.

rows.title: Beginning Painting: Watercolor
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Use color theory, subtractive pigment mixing, and basic drawing skills to produce a series of paintings.
Demonstrate competence in a variety of basic watercolor techniques.
objectives: Explain color theory and subtractive color mixing as it applies to watercolor pigments.
Use assigned limited palettes of various color choices to create a painting.
Demonstrate the use of value to create the illusion of three-dimensional form with simple geometric shapes.
Use subtractive color mixing to create low-intensity colors from high-intensity hues.
Work effectively on dry paper and also wet-into-wet, for hard and soft edges.
Distinguish the expressive differences between various combinations of pigments and techniques.
Create a portfolio of finished, balanced paintings, including background, that demonstrates understanding of the subject and competence in beginning techniques.

rows.title: Advanced Painting: Watercolor
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Reflect upon the creativity of humanity with a meaningful appreciation of the aesthetics of life.
Organize ideas with a sense of the power of design in solving problems.
Collect experiences in art to promote intercultural dialogue.
objectives: Create compositions of a personal nature and style.
Transform creative ideas with new techniques, skills and imagination.
Reflect upon the production of art and compile work for a portfolio review of a personal nature, advanced degree, or professional engagement.

rows.title: Continuing Ceramics
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Create lidded forms and plates using either the pottery wheel or hand building techniques.
Design ceramic forms that utilize slip application to integrate surface of the form.
Articulate the effects of heat upon ceramics, and how heat is measured during firings.
objectives: Upon completion of this course students will be able to create forms that are larger and more complex in design.
Analyze the steps in forming and decorating, and evaluate of results.
Discuss the aesthetics of finished class projects.

rows.title: Beginning Printmaking
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Develop images and designs for printmaking.
Create prints using the printing press and various materials.
Apply the terminology and follow processes of making prints
objectives: Appropriately use printmaking materials, such as tools, drawing materials, plates, and printing papers.
Put into practice various printmaking processes in order to successfully complete editions in black and white.
Practice more non-traditional printmaking processes such as Monotype printmaking and Collograph printmaking.
Operate and use the correct press etiquette with both the intaglio/etching press and the lithographic press.
Apply printmaking history and printmaking technique, and place the information in a contemporary context in their projects
Safe use and disposal of chemicals and hazardous materials used the print making process

rows.title: Mural Design and Creation II
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Demonstrate technical mastery of the steps required to design and paint a mural by completing a grid-based transfer of their black and white drawing to the mural wall, and completing a finished monumental public mural for a community site.
Plan and manage a public celebration connecting the work of the Berkeley City College students and the community for the mural dedication.
objectives: complete a collective black and white and color design proposal for a mural.
write a narrative description of the final mural design and present it to the public in community meeting(s).
discuss the historical background of murals and how that relates to the class mural project.
transfer the black and white drawing of the mural to the wall surface.
use a variety of painting techniques to complete the color rendition on a monumental scale.
document in photo, video and written forms the process of the mural design and creation.
varnish a monumental public mural for a community site.
plan, produce and promote the public inauguration, through press releases, interviews, print and electronic media.
create educational and promotional visual products from the drawings and murals, in the form of post cards, posters, t-shirts or other products.

rows.title: Eco Art Matters Continuing  Food and Water
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Students will explore a variety of materials, develop technical skills, research techniques and practice critical thinking to create proposals and models of their proposed projects
Students will research and use factual data about food and water environmental issues to support art project they propose.
Students will create an artwork or performance that exhibits their personal aesthetic, technical skills and critical thinking and also provides educational information about food and water issues.
objectives: Research information about water and food environmental issues.
Explain relationship between Art and social justice.
Compose a research paper related to Art and Ecology.
Prepare a professional level proposal for creating a public artwork.
Create an educational provocative artwork, installation or performance using materials, technical skills and a personal aesthetic that also informs the public about their chosen issue.
Resaerch exhibition design.
Stage an exhibition reflecting research.
Participate in community outreach events.

rows.title: Advanced Botanical Drawing
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Continue to develop and strengthen personal style, working from traditional and contemporary examples as well as personal preference in subject matter, materials and techniques.
Demonstrate strong facility with creating complex compositions and/or mastery of chosen media and techniques in preparatory sketches and final compositions.
Prepare individual artist statement.
objectives: Demonstrate a thorough understanding and facility with an illustration process of working from combined observational and compositional studies toward a finished illustration showing a high level of understanding and technique.
Begin to develop a personal style, working from traditional and contemporary examples as well as personal preference in subject matter and techniques.
Use professional standards in documenting, labeling and presenting artwork.
Assemble a portfolio of finished work for professional and/or transfer purposes.

rows.title: Ceramics and Digital Technologies
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Demonstrate correct use of terminology as it relates to the ceramic process.
Create CAD designs to fabricate ceramic works or implements.
Demonstrate competency in the creation of ceramic objects using the FabLab and Laney ceramic studio.
objectives: Develop the steps to create an object from design to fabrication.
Describe the project parameters and execute a plan.
Establish a vocabulary to communicate within digital fabrication teams.
Demonstrate safe workplace skills in and around Fablab.
Demonstrate safe practices in and around the ceramic studio.

rows.title: Survey of Art from the Renaissance to Contemporary
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Employ the vocabulary and concepts of formal analysis specific to the visual arts and art history to the art and architecture of the Early Renaissance to the Contempoary Era.
Identify and contextualize artworks from the Early Renaissance to the Contemporary Era according to their formal, iconographic, and social functions.
Analyze the cultural dynamics of art and change from the Early Renaissance to the Contemporary Era.
objectives: Identify, examine, and assess representative works of art and architecture from the Renaissance to the contemporary period employing appropriate art historical terminology.
Analyze works of art and architecture and critique them in terms of aesthetic, socio- political, religious, historical, technological, and cultural contexts in which they were created.
Develop critical thinking, information literacy, and problem solving through an engagement with art, architecture, artists, and patrons from the Renaissance to the contemporary period.

rows.title: Introduction to Asian American and Pacific Islander Studies
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Analyze and evaluate historic and contemporary forms of policy and/or cultural expression related to Asian American and Pacific Islander communities through an analytical lens grounded in AAPI Studies.
Analyze and evaluate Asian American and Pacific Islander experiences in the U.S. as engaged with acts and movements of struggle, resistance, solidarity, and self-determination.
objectives: Identify and analyze Asian American and Pacific Islander contributions to the U.S and the world in the areas of the arts, sciences, history, politics, public policy, and economy.
Contextualize and critique examples of Asian American and Pacific Islander cultural production within a broader sociocultural context

Analyze and articulate concepts such as race and racism, racialization, ethnicity, equity, ethno-centrism, eurocentrism, white supremacy, self-determination, liberation, decolonization, sovereignty, imperialism, settler colonialism, and anti-racism as analyzed in any one or more of the following: Native American Studies, African American Studies, Asian American Studies, and Latina and Latino American Studies.

Critically review how struggle, resistance, racial and social justice, solidarity, and liberation, as experienced and enacted by Native Americans, African Americans, Asian Americans and/or Latina and Latino Americans are relevant to current and structural issues such as communal, national, international, and transnational politics as, for example, in immigration, reparations, settler-colonialism, multiculturalism, language policies.

Describe and actively engage with anti-racist and anti-colonial issues and the practices and movements in Native American, African American, Asian American and/or Latina and Latino communities to build a just and equitable society.

rows.title: Asians and Asian Americans Through Films
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Analyze and critique films and media as a medium of communication and representation of the culture and identity of Asian Americans

Identify and examine common cultural elements, symbols, themes and motifs in films by and about Asian Americans and the Asian Diaspora, Central Asians, East Asians, South Asians, and Southeast Asians.

Compare and contrast cultural issues, historical and political contexts, similarities and differences in values and forms of expression as presented in films by writers, directors and producers from diverse cultures.
Analyze the complex histories of representation and self-representation of Asian Americans and Asian diaspora in the US
objectives: Identify differences between mainstream/commercial and independent films.
Identify, analyze and discuss different film genres, including documentary, drama, comedy and martial arts.
Employ appropriate terminology specific to film studies in critically analyzing films.
Discuss the role of media in influencing one's own perceptual and emotional processes during the film-viewing experience
Analyze the power of media through the use and manipulation of images.
Examine the role of Hollywood in cultural production and the propagation of cultural hegemony.
Compare and contrast Asian cultures and Asian-American cultures in the U.S.
Explore Asian American representations on new digital media platforms
Examine Asian images produced throughout the Asian Diaspora

rows.title: Asian American History to 1945
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Develop civic engagement and leadership through the critical understanding of the diverse history of Asian Americans in the United States.

Develop critical awareness of Asian American experiences in the United States, and the centrality of those experiences in the political and cultural development of the United States through the Second World War.
Engage critically with the diversity of Asian American social, political, and racial experiences through World War II.
objectives: Learn about push and pull factors in immigration and emigration;
Understanding the relationship between immigration and the global economy;
Understand the ethnic stratification pattern in the U.S.;
Grasp the importance of community solidarity to Asian immigrants and their descendants;
Understand the motivation behind racist attacks on Asian Americans;
Understand the relationship between homeland colonization and Asian American communities.

rows.title: American Sign Language IV
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Demonstrate the ASL expressive and receptive functions in advanced level.

Demonstrate the expressive advanced skills of explaining or describing complicated situations and narrating fairy/folk stories, utilizing ASL grammatical features.

Demonstrates proper use of particular language functions (responding to questions or statements appropriately, commanding, requesting, agreeing, etc.) and responds appropriately when conversation partner uses these functions.
Identify the behaviors appropriate to deaf culture through social and language functions.

rows.title: Fingerspelling and Numbers II
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Demonstrate receptive and expressive advanced skills of fingerspelling and numbers.
objectives: Demonstrate the correct form and movement of fingerspelled words.
Demonstrate the correct form and movement of numbers.
Demonstrate the fluency in variation of lexicalized words.
Identify and produce numbers appropriately for various numerical systems in ASL
Understand numbers and fingerspelled words in isolation and brief sentences or stories

rows.title: Engines, Fuel and Ignition Systems
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
outcomes: Disassemble and reassemble a late model automotive engine, including fuel and ignition system, using industry standard practices, manufacturer specifications and both standard and specialized tools as appropriate, including practicing all standard safety procedures.
Demonstrate competence and familiarity with basic and safe engine machining procedures for the servicing of valves, seats, guides, pistons and cylinders.

Demonstrate safe work procedures in the lab;
Perform routine maintenance and adjustments on the above systems, utilizing factory service manuals and reference books and specialized tools when necessary;
Perform disassembly and reassembly operations on automotive engines, utilizing special tools and service manuals as necessary;
Perform minor machine service to heads and blocks, including grinding valves, and seats, knurling and reaming valve guides;
Perform a compression test and explain its results;

Remove, inspect and replace spark plugs and other ignition secondary components; measure ignition timing with a timing light; describe the operation of the ignition system;
